facts.claim: Mondo Cozmo is the performing name of Philadelphia-born, Los Angeles-based singer/songwriter/producer Joshua (Josh) Ostrander.
"Shine" is track 5 on Plastic Soul (4:37). Writer credits go to Joshua Ostrander and Aria Fern Pullman.
Plastic Soul was recorded over about two weeks in Joshua Tree, with only his dog Cozmo for company. Republic Records released it.
Ostrander said he played all the instruments on the album himself, including some he didn't know how to play, and had to figure out the recording alone for the first time after years in bands.
Ostrander said he knew "Shine" was special as soon as he finished the vocal.
"Shine" was one of the songs written during a dark period in his life. It put Mondo Cozmo on the map in late 2016.
"Shine" was Mondo Cozmo's second single, released in September 2016. It peaked at number one on Billboard's Adult Alternative Songs airplay chart.
Ostrander said the video for "Shine" went through about four versions because the label kept saying no. They finally gathered a diverse group of people and shot it.
Before Mondo Cozmo, Ostrander fronted the major-label alt-rock bands Laguardia and Eastern Conference Champions. He also produced other artists.
Ostrander took the name Mondo Cozmo from his dog Cozmo and John Waters' film Mondo Trasho. He wanted a short name that rhymed and looked good on a shirt.

draft:
**Shine** opens as a prayer from someone already on their knees. Mondo Cozmo's Josh Ostrander asks Jesus to stay with him through a coming storm, admits he's come looking for something he lost, and then starts to bargain: "I promise you I will return if you take me back." That line is the whole first verse in small. It's a deal offered by someone who isn't sure they deserve one, the voice of a person who has left before and knows it.

Then the song turns outward, and that's where it gets generous. The second verse stops pleading for himself and starts worrying about everyone else: "My friends don't understand that we all are lost." He doesn't set himself above them. The "we" puts him in the same ditch. The refrain that follows, letting them get high and letting them get stoned, could read like a shrug. Set against those verses it sounds like mercy. He isn't going to lecture anyone. He's going to pray for them and leave them be. The guilt in the bargain and the tenderness in the refrain never settle into one feeling. Both stay in the room.

Ostrander has said "Shine" was one of the songs he wrote during a dark period, and the delivery carries that. His voice is slightly raspy and mid-range, held long and pushed almost to a shout, with a higher harmony climbing in beside him. The band moves at a moderate, driving rock pace: a prominent snare, a simple bass line keeping the floor steady, clean electric guitar holding sustained chords, and keyboard pads filling in underneath. The production is polished and full, and the arrangement builds. Here that "band" is Ostrander himself. He made the album, *Plastic Soul*, over about two weeks in Joshua Tree with only his dog Cozmo for company, playing every instrument, some he didn't know how to play. It was his first time recording alone after years fronting Laguardia and Eastern Conference Champions. He said he knew the song was special as soon as he finished the vocal.

The lineage is Arcade Fire's kind of anthem, built for big rooms and shouted together, with a Dylanesque plainness in how the verses talk straight to God. It landed squarely in adult alternative radio and went to number one on Billboard's Adult Alternative Songs chart. The writing, credited to Ostrander and Aria Fern Pullman, saves its last verse for one more plea. He asks Mary to walk with him through these modern lies and asks to be held and never let go. Then the song gives itself over to the refrain, again and again, with voices answering each other: "Everything will be alright if you let it go."

It sticks because it lets you pray for your own lost friends without judging them, and by the tenth time through that refrain you've stopped judging yourself too.
